intro:
## Beep... beep... beep-beep-beep!

Lots of cars have a **parking sensor** in the back bumper. As the car reverses towards a wall, it beeps faster and faster. When the car is really close, the beep turns into one long tone: **stop!**

The sensor is an **ultrasonic distance sensor** (the HC-SR04). It sends out a squeak too high for people to hear, then times how long the echo takes to come back. A short echo means something is close.

You'll build your own, one part at a time:
- test the **sensor** on its own: measure distances in centimetres
- test the **three lights** on their own
- join them: **green**, **amber** and **red** zones
- test the **buzzer** on its own
- join it to the sensor: **beep faster** as you get closer
- put it all together, then play a **parking game**

**In the Simulator:** drag the slider under the sensor on the board. Left is closer, right is further away.

**Safety:**
- Take the **blue HAT off** before you change any wires, and put it back on after.
- **Never turn the Pi off**, or you'll lose your progress.
- The sensor's ECHO pin sends back **5V**, which is too much for a GPIO pin. It must go through the **two resistors** (see **Wiring + Safety**). Ask your teacher to check them before you put the blue HAT back on.
outro:
## Parked perfectly!

You built a real car gadget. You used a **sensor** that measures distance, **if / elif / else** to sort numbers into zones, a **variable** that remembers the last zone, and **timing** you control yourself with `sleep()`.

**In the real world:** car parking sensors work just like yours. Ultrasonic sensors in the bumper measure the distance many times a second, and a little computer turns it into beeps and coloured bars on the dashboard. Robot vacuums, drones and automatic doors use the same idea.

**Extension ideas:**
- Keep a **closest ever** record, and use the button to reset it
- Show the distance as a bar of `#` symbols that shrinks as you get closer: `print("#" * round(cm / 5))`
- Make **two players** take turns at the parking game, and print the winner

steps.text:
Every parking sensor starts with one part: the thing that measures distance. Build the sensor first (see **Wiring + Safety**).

`DistanceSensor(echo=26, trigger=4)` is the sensor. **TRIG** on GPIO4 sends the squeak. **ECHO** on GPIO26 hears it come back.

`sensor.distance` is how far away the nearest thing is, in **metres**, from 0 up to 1. There are 100 centimetres in a metre, so times 100 gives **centimetres**.

**Your task:** fill in the blank so the program prints centimetres. Run it, and while it counts, move something closer and further away.

*Simulator:* drag the slider under the sensor on the board. *Real Pi:* move a book or your hand in front of the sensor.

from gpiozero import DistanceSensor, LED
from time import sleep

sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=26, trigger=4)
red = LED(17)
amber = LED(27)
green = LED(22)

print("Parking sensor on. Come closer!")
while True:
    cm = sensor.distance * 100
    green.off()
    amber.off()
    red.off()
    if cm > 60:
        green.on()          # lots of room
    elif cm >= 20:
        amber.on()          # getting close
    else:
        red.on()            # very close!
    sleep(0.1)

steps.text:
Now join the sensor and the lights. A parking sensor sorts the distance into **zones**:

- more than **60 cm**: green, lots of room
- **20 to 60 cm**: amber, getting close
- less than **20 cm**: red, very close!

The `while True` loop measures the distance 10 times a second. Each time, it turns all the lights off, then `if / elif / else` turns the right one on.

Python checks `if`, then `elif`, then `else`, **in order**, and stops at the first one that's true. So by the time it gets to `elif`, it already knows the distance isn't more than 60.

**Your task:** fill in the two blanks: amber when the distance is **20 cm or more**, and red for everything else. Run it, move closer and further away, then press **Stop**.

steps.text:
The last part is the **buzzer**. Build it (see **Wiring + Safety**). Your zones code is safe in `backups/`.

`buzzer.beep(0.1, 0.5, n=4, background=False)` beeps **4 times**. The first number is the **on time** (0.1 seconds of sound). The second is the **off time** (0.5 seconds of quiet). `background=False` means your program waits until the beeping is finished.

A shorter off time means faster beeps. That's the trick a parking sensor uses!

**Your task:** fill in the blank so the second lot of beeps is **faster**: give it a shorter off time than 0.5. Run it and listen.

steps.text:
Join the sensor and the buzzer. The closer you get, the **shorter the gap** between beeps.

You might think: just call `buzzer.beep()` every time round the loop. But `beep()` runs in the **background** with its own timer. Calling it again restarts it before it has finished, so the beeps get muddled.

So this time **your code** makes each beep, with `sleep()`:
- `buzzer.on()`, a short `sleep(0.05)`, then `buzzer.off()`: one short beep
- then a quiet gap of `sleep(cm / 100)`. At 100 cm that's 1 second. At 20 cm it's only 0.2 seconds!
- closer than **10 cm**, the buzzer just stays on: one long tone means **stop!**

**Your task:** fill in the two blanks: a long tone when the distance is **less than 10**, and a gap of **cm divided by 100**. Run it and move slowly closer. Get closer than 10 cm, then press **Stop**.

steps.text:
Time to put it all together! This program joins your lights from step 3 and your beeps from step 5. (Your step 5 code is safe in `backups/`.)

Did you notice the Output filling up in step 5? A real dashboard doesn't shout the distance 10 times a second. Let's only print when something **changes**.

Each zone now has a name, like `"getting close"`. The variable `last_zone` **remembers** the zone from last time round the loop:
- if `zone` is **not the same** as `last_zone` (`!=` means "is not equal to"), something changed: print it
- then set `last_zone` to the new zone, so it won't print again until the zone changes

**Your task:** fill in the two blanks so it prints only when the zone changes. Run it, drive slowly up to the "wall" until it says `STOP!`, then back away. Press **Stop**.

steps.demo:
from gpiozero import DistanceSensor, LED, Buzzer, Button
from time import sleep

sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=26, trigger=4)
red = LED(17)
amber = LED(27)
green = LED(22)
buzzer = Buzzer(18)
button = Button(23)
last_zone = ""
score = 0

def park():
    global score
    cm = sensor.distance * 100
    if cm < 10:
        print("Crash! Too close.")
    elif cm <= 20:
        print("Perfect park!")
        score += 1
    else:
        print("Too far from the wall.")
    print("Score:", score)

button.when_pressed = park
print("Drive up to the wall, then press the button to park.")

while True:
    cm = sensor.distance * 100

    green.off()
    amber.off()
    red.off()
    if cm > 60:
        zone = "all clear"
        green.on()
    elif cm >= 20:
        zone = "getting close"
        amber.on()
    elif cm >= 10:
        zone = "very close"
        red.on()
    else:
        zone = "STOP!"
        red.on()

    if zone != last_zone:
        print(round(cm), "cm:", zone)
        last_zone = zone

    if cm < 10:
        buzzer.on()
        sleep(0.1)
    else:
        buzzer.on()
        sleep(0.05)
        buzzer.off()
        sleep(cm / 100)

Then `elif cm <= 20:` prints `Perfect park!` and does `score += 1`. `else:` prints `Too far from the wall.` Last line of `park()`: `print("Score:", score)`.

steps.text:
Turn your parking sensor into a game! Drive up to the wall, stop where you think is perfect, and press the **park button**.

**Goal:** when the button on GPIO23 is pressed, check the distance and print how you went:
- closer than 10 cm: `Crash! Too close.`
- 10 to 20 cm: `Perfect park!`, and add 1 to a **score**
- further than 20 cm: `Too far from the wall.`

Then print the score, like `Score: 2`.

**Tips:**
- Import `Button` too, and make `button = Button(23)` near the top
- `score = 0` near the top. A function that changes it needs `global score` as its first line
- Write `def park():` that measures `cm` itself, then uses `if / elif / else`
- Connect it before the loop: `button.when_pressed = park` (no brackets!)

**Bonus:** keep a **closest ever** record, or give a "Wow, centimetre perfect!" message for exactly 15 cm.
steps.title: Challenge: the parking game

title: Parking Sensor

wiring.connect: VCC → 5V (pin 2). GND → GND (pin 6). TRIG → GPIO4 (pin 7). ECHO → 1kΩ resistor → GPIO26 (pin 37), plus a 2kΩ resistor from GPIO26 to GND. The two resistors turn the 5V echo into a safe 3.3V.
GPIO17 (pin 11) → 330Ω resistor → LED long leg (+). Short leg (−) → GND rail.
GPIO27 (pin 13) → 330Ω resistor → LED long leg (+). Short leg (−) → GND rail.
GPIO22 (pin 15) → 330Ω resistor → LED long leg (+). Short leg (−) → GND rail.
An *active* buzzer: + (the longer leg) → GPIO18 (pin 12). − → GND rail.
One leg → GPIO23 (pin 16). The leg across the middle gap → GND rail. (Only needed for the challenge in step 7.)
Got a 3.3V sensor (HC-SR04P or RCWL-1601)? Power it from 3V3 (pin 1) instead, and you can leave out the two resistors. Point the sensor at an open space, and use a book or your hand as the wall.
